title: Cooking Slum Gullion for 54 musicians at the Three Deuces
summary: Leeman and Harold West swap sets on Sundays so each can cook; Leeman's pot of Slum Gullion feeds musicians including Charlie Parker and Dizzy, while West tops him with soul food.

story.theme_name: Coming to New York: clubs, jams, and making it
story.community_name: Making it in New York: arrival, clubs and the scene

blocks.x: One incident of note -- I had an arrangement with Harold West, an excellent soul food cook -- that was his hobby, as well as mine. I have been cooking since I was a kid. I started actually cooking on the road because I loved my grandmother's food, and as a kid on the road, I missed that New England home cooking, so I had to cook it myself to remind me of home.

However, back to the Deuces -- Harold West and I came to -- had an arrangement where he played some of my sets on one Sunday while I cooked, and I'd reciprocate and cover him on his sets the following Sunday while he cooked.

They didn't serve food in the Deuces, because they couldn't afford a regular cook, a chef. So I had a beautiful kitchen all to myself for the first time in my life -- with huge ranges, 10, 15 and 20 gallon pots. Just shining, steel pots -- the works, and I was thrilled.

I paid -- I went shopping on Sunday morning, and I got at the club at 10 AM, I had gone down to the Italian section, which was open on Sundays, and this is the first Sunday I cooked, and I made 10 to 15 gallons of Slum Gullion* Now this was something I developed over the years, which is elbow macaroni with bits of ground beef and steak and Italian sausages and peppers, cheese and what have you, and with a light tomato and garlic sauce (Gee, and I'm getting hungry now!) mixed in all together, and I put it in the warmer, the steamer, and made another huge mixed salad. I made a huge mixed salad in a ten pound container, and several loaves of French Italian bread, and I left a dish and a sign on the kitchen table, reading, "Wash your own pets and dishes and don't forget to feed the kitty."

All day long the kitchen got busy, and as word passed around the street, Charlie Parker ducked in, Dizzy Gillespie, Ben Webster, countless musicians of the era that were developing their styles, especially Dizzy with his "salted peanuts," he was still working on them.
And only a few of my patrons -- I think Charlie

Parker came in for threesies. And there were only a few -- the guys playing on the street were only a few of my patrons because there were a gang of musicians at the White Rose as the word spread, and the food was all gone before closing -- and I made, and I just about broke even with the kitty; I think I was $25 in there, food was much cheaper then. But I cooked for a lot of people -- I think we counted 54 guys in all.

And I'll close this by saying the following Sunday, Harold West wiped my reputation off the slate. He made pigs feet and lima beans, and ham hocks, and the likes that I had never tasted before. And I played a couple of sets with Earl and Slam, he added insult to injury of baking, from scratch, biscuits and cornbread. Whew.
